title: Energy Resources: Renewable, Non-renewable and Green Energy

questions.stem: Sort these energy resources into renewable and non-renewable.
questions.explanation: Renewable resources are replaced by nature and will not run out. Coal, oil and natural gas took millions of years to form, and uranium (nuclear fuel) is also limited.

questions.stem: Natural gas is a renewable resource.
questions.explanation: Natural gas is a fossil fuel. It formed over millions of years and we use it much faster than it forms, so it will run out.

questions.stem: Burning fossil fuels releases ___ ___ (CO₂), a greenhouse gas that traps heat in the air.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide traps heat, so more of it in the air leads to climate change.

questions.stem: A renewable energy resource is one that…
options: formed from buried plants over millions of years
is made in a factory and sold in shops
is replaced naturally and will not run out
can be used only once by one power station
questions.explanation: Sunlight, wind and moving water are renewable. The resource formed from buried plants over millions of years describes a fossil fuel, which is non-renewable.

questions.stem: Match each energy resource to what it comes from.
pairs: plants buried for millions of years
questions.explanation: Renewable resources come from the Sun, the wind, water, living things or heat inside the Earth. Coal is a fossil fuel made from plants buried for millions of years.

questions.stem: Nuclear power stations release a lot of carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: They release almost none. But nuclear fuel (uranium) is non-renewable and the waste is dangerous.

questions.stem: Which of these are green energy choices? Choose all that are right.
options: solar panels
wind turbines
burning more coal
LED bulbs that use less energy
leaving fans on in empty rooms
questions.explanation: Solar and wind release little or no pollution, and using energy efficiently is green too. Burning coal and wasting electricity do the opposite.

questions.stem: Put the steps in order to show how burning fossil fuels causes climate change.
sequence: Coal, oil or gas is burned.
Carbon dioxide is released into the air.
The extra carbon dioxide traps more heat.
The Earth warms and the climate changes.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide trap heat, so more of them means a warmer Earth, with changes such as stronger cyclones and rising seas.

questions.stem: Why is burning fossil fuels a **global** problem?
options: It only harms the town where the fuel is burned.
The carbon dioxide spreads through the air and affects the whole planet.
It makes all the fuel renewable.
It makes the air colder everywhere.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from any country mixes in the air and traps heat everywhere. That is why countries must act together.

questions.stem: Why is Bangladesh one of the countries most at risk from climate change?
questions.model_answer: Climate change brings stronger cyclones, floods and rising sea levels, and Bangladesh is low and has a long coast.
questions.explanation: Bangladesh faces stronger cyclones, floods and sea-level rise along the coast, which put homes, farms and lives at risk.

questions.stem: About 685 million people in the world still had no electricity at home in 2022 (Tracking SDG7). In which region do most of them live?
options: Sub-Saharan Africa
North America
Australia
Europe
questions.explanation: Most people without electricity live in Sub-Saharan Africa. Energy access is a global issue as well as a climate issue.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a source of green energy?
questions.explanation: Wind turbines use renewable wind and release no smoke. The other pictures show pollution from burning or using fossil fuels.

questions.stem: Match each picture to the energy it uses.
questions.explanation: Solar, wind and hydro use sunlight, moving air and moving water. A nuclear power station uses uranium, which is non-renewable.

questions.stem: Which pictures show things that put smoke or fumes into the air? Choose all that are right.
questions.explanation: Factories and cars burning fossil fuels release smoke, fumes and carbon dioxide. Solar panels, wind turbines and bicycles do not.

questions.stem: Which picture shows a hazard that climate change is making worse for Bangladesh?
questions.explanation: Climate change brings stronger cyclones, floods and sea-level rise to Bangladesh. Volcanoes, snow and deserts are not the main risks.

questions.stem: A hydro power station makes electricity using which of these?
questions.explanation: Hydro means water. Moving water turns a generator to make electricity, as at the Kaptai plant on the Karnaphuli River.

questions.stem: Rafi’s school wants to cut its electricity bill. Which change helps most without lowering learning?
options: leave the lights on all day
swap old bulbs for LED bulbs
run the computers overnight
buy more fans and keep them on
questions.explanation: LED bulbs give the same light with less electricity. The cleanest energy is the energy we do not waste.

questions.stem: A family on a remote char far from the national grid wants clean electricity for lights and a phone charger. What is a good choice?
options: a coal-fired generator
a big hydro dam
a solar home system
a nuclear power station
questions.explanation: Solar home systems use sunlight, release no pollution, and are already used by millions of homes in Bangladesh. The other options are far too large or polluting for one family.

questions.stem: Anika switches off the fan and lights when she leaves an empty classroom. This saves electricity and helps to cut carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: Much of our electricity still comes from fossil fuels. Using less electricity means less fuel is burned.

questions.stem: The school wants to cut its electricity bill and its carbon footprint. Which actions would help? Choose all that are right.
options: put solar panels on the roof
use LED bulbs
switch off fans and lights in empty rooms
leave the computers on overnight
use old bulbs that waste more energy
questions.explanation: Solar panels give clean electricity, and LED bulbs and switching off save energy. Leaving things on or using wasteful bulbs does the opposite.

questions.stem: Nadia’s family in a village keeps cows. How could they get a renewable fuel for cooking?
options: collecting natural gas from the ground
burning plastic bottles
buying coal from the market
a biogas plant that uses dung
questions.explanation: Biogas is made from animal dung and plants, so it can be replaced all the time. Coal and natural gas are fossil fuels, and burning plastic is harmful.

questions.stem: In the simulation, what happens to the temperature when you add more greenhouse gases to the air?

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Turn on the sunlight. Watch the thermometer, then add more greenhouse gases to the air and watch again.

options: It goes up.
It goes down.
It stays exactly the same.
It goes up and then falls back to zero.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases trap heat that tries to escape from the ground, so the air warms. This is why burning fossil fuels causes climate change.

questions.stem: In the simulation, with more greenhouse gases in the air, more of the heat (infrared) rising from the ground is trapped instead of escaping.

sim.task: Open Greenhouse Effect. Turn on the sunlight. Compare the heat (infrared) rays leaving the ground with only a little gas in the air and with a lot of greenhouse gas.

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases absorb the heat rays and send some back down. More gas means more heat is trapped.

questions.stem: Put the energy chain in order for a solar panel lighting a bulb.

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the Sun as the source, a solar panel as the energy changer and a light bulb as the user. Watch where the energy goes.

sequence: Sunlight shines on the solar panel.
The solar panel changes the light into electricity.
Electricity flows to the light bulb.
questions.explanation: The Sun is the energy source, the solar panel changes the energy, and the bulb uses it. Sunlight is a renewable resource.

questions.stem: In the simulation, running water turns the generator and the light bulb lights up. Which kind of power station does this copy?

sim.task: Open Energy Forms and Changes and choose the Systems screen. Choose the tap with running water as the source, the generator as the energy changer and a light bulb as the user. Watch the generator and the bulb.

options: a solar power station
a hydro power station
a nuclear power station
a coal power station
questions.explanation: Moving water turns the generator, just as in a hydro plant like Kaptai. Water is a renewable resource.

questions.stem: World electricity in 2024 (Ember, rounded): coal 34%, gas 22%, other fossil 3%, nuclear 9%, hydro 14%, wind 8%, solar 7%, other renewable 3%. Which statements are right? Choose all that are right.
options: Fossil fuels together made about 59%.
Wind and solar together made more electricity than hydro.
Nuclear and all renewables together made about 41%.
Gas made more electricity than coal.
Hydro, wind, solar and other renewables together made more than coal.
questions.explanation: 34 + 22 + 3 = 59%. Wind + solar = 15%, which is more than hydro (14%). Nuclear 9 + renewables 32 = 41%. Coal (34%) beat gas (22%), and renewables (32%) were just below coal.

questions.stem: Bangladesh made 55% of its electricity from natural gas, 20% from oil, 14% from coal and 11% from imports, hydro and solar (2023, PGCB data reported by Reuters). The world made 22% from gas and 34% from coal (2024, Ember). Which comparison is correct?
options: Bangladesh made over half its electricity from renewables.
Bangladesh used a bigger share of coal than the world did.
Bangladesh used a bigger share of gas than the world did.
The world made most of its electricity from gas.
questions.explanation: 55% is bigger than 22% for gas. For coal, Bangladesh (14%) used a smaller share than the world (34%). Neither made most of its electricity from renewables.

questions.stem: In 2023 Bangladesh made 55% of its electricity from natural gas, 20% from oil and 14% from coal (PGCB data reported by Reuters). Together, fossil fuels made ___ % of its electricity.
questions.explanation: 55 + 20 + 14 = 89%. Only about 11% came from imports, hydro and solar, so Bangladesh depends heavily on fossil fuels.

questions.stem: Class 5A tested a paper wind turbine with 6 blades in front of a fan (example data). The turns in 30 seconds were 52, 55 and 55. The mean number of turns is ___.
questions.explanation: 52 + 55 + 55 = 162, and 162 ÷ 3 = 54. Repeating a test and finding the mean makes results more reliable.

questions.stem: Class 5A’s mean turns in 30 seconds (example data): 2 blades 40, 3 blades 56, 4 blades 61, 6 blades 54, 8 blades 44. Describe the pattern and explain why more blades are not always better.
questions.model_answer: The speed rose up to 4 blades and then fell. More blades catch more wind, but too many add weight and block the air.
questions.explanation: The best result was 61 turns with 4 blades. After that extra blades made the turbine heavier and got in each other’s way, so it turned more slowly.
